lesson.summary: A **data logger** is just a sensor reading, wrapped in a loop, with a **timestamp** attached, saved somewhere you can look at later.
lesson.content:
## Project: Simple Data Logger

> **Core Concept:** A **data logger** is just a sensor reading, wrapped in a loop, with a **timestamp** attached, saved somewhere you can look at later.

### Why It Matters
- Reading a sensor once is easy, reading it **consistently over time** and keeping a record of it is what actually turns raw readings into useful data.
- This project is a beginner-friendly stand-in for a real SD card logger, using the **Serial Monitor** as a simple, buildable substitute.
- It's the pattern behind real projects like tracking a room's temperature overnight or logging light levels across a day.

### Intuitive Analogy
This is like keeping a fitness journal instead of just glancing at a scale
once. One weigh-in tells you almost nothing on its own, but writing down
the number every morning, with the date next to it, turns a single
snapshot into a trend you can actually learn from. A data logger does the
exact same thing for a sensor, one reading at a time, with a timestamp,
building up a record instead of a single glance.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: any sensor you already know how to read (a temperature sensor or potentiometer works fine), and your microcontroller board.
- Instead of writing to an SD card, which needs extra hardware and a library, print each reading to the Serial Monitor, that's your beginner-friendly 'log file' for now.
- Track elapsed time with **millis()**, which counts milliseconds since the board powered on, no real-time clock module required for a basic version.
- Each loop pass: read the sensor, read the current millis() value, and print both together on one line, separated clearly, ideally with a consistent delimiter like a comma, so they're easy to scan or later import into a spreadsheet.
- Use a fixed delay() between readings, like every 2 seconds, so your log has evenly spaced data points instead of random gaps, which matters a lot if you ever want to graph the data.
- Copying the Serial Monitor's output into a text file afterward gives you a simple log you can open, review, or even graph later in a spreadsheet program.
- millis() is stored as an unsigned long and will eventually ==wrap back around to zero== after about 49 days of continuous uptime, a detail that matters for very long-running loggers but is safe to ignore for short sessions.
- A **comma-separated format** (CSV-style: timestamp,reading) is a small habit worth building early, since it lets you drop the exact same log text straight into a spreadsheet without reformatting it by hand.
- The Serial Monitor's buffer is ==not permanent storage==, closing it, or losing power, throws away everything unless you copied the data out or are logging to a persistent medium like an SD card or a connected computer capturing the serial output.
- This same read, timestamp, print, wait pattern extends directly to real long-term loggers: swap millis() for a real-time clock module and Serial.print() for writes to an SD card file, and the core loop barely changes.

topics.title: Project: A Simple Metronome
topics.description: A **potentiometer** lets a human turn a knob and change your program's timing live, without ever touching the code again.

lesson.summary: A **potentiometer** lets a human turn a knob and change your program's timing live, without ever touching the code again.
lesson.content:
## Project: A Simple Metronome

> **Core Concept:** A **potentiometer** lets a human turn a knob and change your program's timing live, without ever touching the code again.

### Why It Matters
- So far every timing value (every delay()) has been hardcoded, this project makes tempo something a person can adjust in real time.
- It combines nearly everything from earlier projects: analogRead() from the night light, digitalWrite() from the blinking LED, and a buzzer output from the alarm.
- A metronome is also a genuinely satisfying finished project, since the effect of turning the knob is instant and obvious.

### Intuitive Analogy
A potentiometer is like a volume knob, except instead of controlling
loudness, you're using it to control speed. Turn it one way and the
microcontroller reads a small number and beats fast, turn it the other
way and it reads a large number and beats slow. The knob never talks
directly to the buzzer, it only ever talks to the code, which decides
what to do with that number.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one potentiometer, one buzzer or LED as the beat indicator, a resistor if using an LED, jumper wires, breadboard.
- Potentiometer wiring: one outer pin to 5V, the other outer pin to ground, and the middle pin (the wiper) to an analog input pin.
- A potentiometer is really just two resistors back to back, sharing a middle contact, turning the knob shifts how much resistance sits above the wiper versus below it, which is exactly what shifts the wiper's voltage.
- That middle pin's voltage slides between 5V and 0V as you turn the knob, which analogRead() reports as a number from 0 to 1023, the same style of reading used for the LDR in the night light project.
- In code, **map()** converts that raw 0 to 1023 reading into a more useful range, like 100 to 1000 milliseconds, for the beat interval. map() does this with straightforward proportional scaling, it does ==not smooth or filter== the reading in any way.
- loop() reads the knob, converts it to a beat interval, then briefly pulses the buzzer or LED on and off using that interval as the delay().
- Because the knob is read fresh every pass through loop(), the tempo changes live as you turn it, no re-upload needed.
- A wider mapped range (say 100 to 1200 milliseconds) makes the knob feel dramatic across its whole turn, a narrow range (say 480 to 520 milliseconds) makes most of the knob's travel ==barely noticeable==, choosing that range is a real design decision, not just an implementation detail.
- Musically, beats per minute (BPM) and milliseconds per beat are just inverses of each other, 60,000 divided by the millisecond interval gives BPM, useful if you ever want to show a real tempo number instead of just a raw delay value.

topics.title: Project: Temperature Display
topics.description: Turning a raw **analog voltage** from a temperature sensor into a real number you can read is the core skill behind every sensor-based project.

lesson.summary: Turning a raw **analog voltage** from a temperature sensor into a real number you can read is the core skill behind every sensor-based project.
lesson.content:
## Project: Temperature Display

> **Core Concept:** Turning a raw **analog voltage** from a temperature sensor into a real number you can read is the core skill behind every sensor-based project.

### Why It Matters
- Most sensors don't hand you a clean number like '72 degrees', they hand you a **raw voltage** that you have to convert yourself.
- This project is the first time you combine analogRead with real math instead of just checking if a pin is HIGH or LOW.
- It's a beginner-friendly stand-in for any 'read a sensor, show the value' display project, like a thermostat or weather station.

### Intuitive Analogy
A temperature sensor is like a bathroom scale that only shows you a dial
position, not a number. It's on you to read where the needle sits and
translate that into "68 kilograms." Your microcontroller does the same
thing: it reads a raw dial position (a voltage) off the sensor pin, and
your code is the part that translates that position into "72 degrees" you
can actually understand.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: a TMP36 (or similar) analog temperature sensor, three jumper wires, and your microcontroller board. No soldering required, the TMP36 has three legs: power, signal, and ground, arranged in a flat row on most packages.
- Wiring: sensor's power leg to 5V, ground leg to GND, and the middle signal leg to an analog input pin (like A0). Getting the flat side of the sensor facing you and matching the datasheet's pinout matters, the three legs are not interchangeable.
- In code, analogRead() gives back a raw integer from 0 to 1023 representing the voltage on that pin, where 0 means 0V and 1023 means the board's **reference voltage**, usually 5V or 3.3V depending on the board.
- That raw number gets converted to actual voltage with a formula (raw divided by 1023, times the reference voltage), then that voltage gets converted to degrees Celsius using the sensor's datasheet formula, which for the TMP36 is **(voltage minus 0.5) times 100**.
- The ==0.5V offset== in the TMP36's formula exists so the sensor can represent temperatures below freezing with a positive voltage instead of needing a negative one, which analogRead() cannot measure at all.
- Instead of a physical display, print the temperature to the Serial Monitor every second, a beginner-friendly stand-in for an LCD or seven-segment display, and a good way to confirm your math before adding real display hardware.
- Wrap the read, convert, and print steps in loop() with a short delay so the reading updates continuously without flooding the screen with thousands of near-identical lines.
- Converting Celsius to Fahrenheit afterward, with tempF = tempC times 9/5 plus 32, is a one-line addition once the Celsius math already works, and a good way to check the code produces sensible real-world numbers.
- Averaging several consecutive readings before printing smooths out small jitter from electrical noise, which matters more once you start comparing readings over time rather than just watching one number update.
- Every analog sensor in this course follows the same three-stage shape you're practicing here: read a raw number, convert it with a formula from the datasheet, then use the result. Learning this pattern once makes every future sensor project faster to build.

topics.title: Project: A Tiny Traffic Light
topics.description: Three LEDs on a timed sequence turn a single blink into a small **state machine**, the real building block behind most embedded projects.

lesson.summary: Three LEDs on a timed sequence turn a single blink into a small **state machine**, the real building block behind most embedded projects.
lesson.content:
## Project: A Tiny Traffic Light

> **Core Concept:** Three LEDs on a timed sequence turn a single blink into a small **state machine**, the real building block behind most embedded projects.

### Why It Matters
- Real devices rarely control just one output, they coordinate several outputs in a specific order, and a traffic light is the cleanest example of that.
- This project builds directly on the blinking LED skills, but stacks them: three pins instead of one, each with its own timing.
- It's a natural first step toward thinking in 'states' (red, then yellow, then green) instead of just on and off.

### Intuitive Analogy
A single blinking LED is like flipping a light switch. A traffic light is
more like a stage manager running a show: red is act one, yellow is a
short transition, green is act two, and the manager always knows exactly
which act comes next and how long it should run before cueing the next one.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: one red LED, one yellow LED, one green LED, three resistors (around 220 ohm each), jumper wires, breadboard.
- Wiring: each LED gets its own output pin through its own resistor to its anode, with all three cathodes sharing a common ground. Three independent branches off shared power and ground rails, not three LEDs chained one after another.
- In code, declare three pin numbers and set all three as OUTPUT in setup(). Each pin is completely independent from the microcontroller's point of view, driving one HIGH or LOW never affects the others.
- The core logic in loop() is just a repeating sequence: turn red on, wait, turn red off and yellow on, wait, turn yellow off and green on, wait, turn green off, then start over.
- Real traffic lights hold red and green much longer than yellow, mirror that with different delay() values for each stage instead of one fixed delay.
- This is your first '**cycle**': the sequence always returns to its starting state and repeats indefinitely, the same shape (a fixed loop of states) that shows up again and again in embedded programming.
- Because delay() ==blocks everything==, the whole board is effectively frozen, unable to react to anything else, for the entire 3 seconds red is lit. This is fine for a self-contained toy but is the first hint of why bigger projects eventually move away from delay().
- Each LED needing its own resistor, even though all three share one ground, is the same current-limiting logic from the blinking LED project applied three times over, not a new rule.
- You can verify wiring mistakes fast here: if a color never lights, check its resistor and pin number first, if two colors are always lit together, check for a short or a pin number typo.

topics.title: Project: Ultrasonic Distance Sensor
topics.description: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by **timing** how long a sound pulse takes to bounce back, then doing simple speed-of-sound math.

lesson.summary: An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by **timing** how long a sound pulse takes to bounce back, then doing simple speed-of-sound math.
lesson.content:
## Project: Ultrasonic Distance Sensor

> **Core Concept:** An ultrasonic sensor measures distance by **timing** how long a sound pulse takes to bounce back, then doing simple speed-of-sound math.

### Why It Matters
- Measuring distance without touching anything is a core building block for robots that need to avoid obstacles, or sensors that beep as you back up a car.
- It's the first project where the sensor's 'reading' is actually a **time measurement**, not a voltage, which is a genuinely different way of thinking about a sensor.
- Getting the timing and math right teaches you to read a datasheet carefully instead of guessing at pin behavior.

### Intuitive Analogy
This is exactly how a bat finds a wall in the dark, or how you'd measure a
canyon's depth by yelling and timing the echo. Send a short "ping" out,
start a stopwatch, and stop it the instant the echo comes back. Sound
travels at a known, steady speed, so that travel time alone is enough to
calculate exactly how far away the object was.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Parts needed: an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor (or similar), four jumper wires, and your microcontroller board. The HC-SR04 has two round transducers on its front, one that emits the ultrasonic pulse and one that listens for the echo.
- Wiring: sensor's VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG pin to one digital output pin, ECHO pin to one digital input pin. TRIG and ECHO are two separate pins doing two separate jobs, not a single shared line.
- In code, send a short HIGH pulse on the TRIG pin, this tells the sensor to emit its ultrasonic ping, a burst of sound above the range of human hearing, typically around 40kHz.
- Then use pulseIn() on the ECHO pin, which measures exactly how long that pin stays HIGH, that duration is the **round trip travel time** of the sound out to the object and back.
- Convert that travel time to distance using the speed of sound (about **343 meters per second**, or 0.0343 centimeters per microsecond, at room temperature), and remember to ==divide by two== since the sound traveled to the object and back, not just one way.
- Print the distance to the Serial Monitor in a loop, with a short delay so readings stay steady and readable and the previous echo has time to fully settle.
- The speed of sound changes slightly with air temperature and humidity, so a distance sensor's accuracy has a small built-in margin of error unless you compensate for temperature separately, which most beginner projects skip.
- Very close objects (often under about 2cm) and very far or angled objects can produce unreliable or missing echoes, since the sound needs to bounce mostly straight back to the receiver to be detected at all.
- pulseIn() has an optional ==timeout== parameter, without one it will block your code indefinitely waiting for a pulse that never arrives if no echo comes back, which matters if an object is out of range or angled away.
- Soft, angled, or sound-absorbing surfaces (like foam or thick fabric) scatter or absorb the ping instead of reflecting it cleanly, which can make the sensor report no object even when one is physically present.

topics.title: Project: A Wireless Sensor Node
topics.description: A battery-powered sensor node reads a value, sends it wirelessly, then **sleeps** to save power, since it has no wall outlet to lean on.

lesson.summary: A battery-powered sensor node reads a value, sends it wirelessly, then **sleeps** to save power, since it has no wall outlet to lean on.
lesson.content:
## Project: A Wireless Sensor Node

> **Core Concept:** A battery-powered sensor node reads a value, sends it wirelessly, then **sleeps** to save power, since it has no wall outlet to lean on.

### Why It Matters
- You want to measure something (temperature, soil moisture, motion) somewhere there's no convenient power outlet or wire run.
- A board running WiFi at full power constantly drains a battery in hours, not the weeks or months you actually want.
- Sending every single reading the instant it's taken wastes both power and bandwidth for data that barely changed.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a wireless sensor node like a scout who checks in by radio instead
of staying on the line all day. The scout doesn't keep the radio on
constantly, that would drain their battery pack fast. Instead they nap,
wake up, take a quick look around, radio back a short report, and go right
back to napping. The person listening only hears from them occasionally,
but that's exactly enough to know what's going on.


### Key Engineering Principles

topics.title: Reading a Datasheet Without Panicking
topics.description: A **datasheet** is just a component's spec sheet, and as a beginner you only need to find a handful of numbers on it, not read the whole thing.

lesson.summary: A **datasheet** is just a component's spec sheet, and as a beginner you only need to find a handful of numbers on it, not read the whole thing.
lesson.content:
## Reading a Datasheet Without Panicking

> **Core Concept:** A **datasheet** is just a component's spec sheet, and as a beginner you only need to find a handful of numbers on it, not read the whole thing.

### Why It Matters
- Datasheets are often dozens of pages long, dense with graphs and tables that look intimidating before you know what to ignore.
- Skipping datasheets entirely leads to ==guessing values==, which is exactly how components get damaged or circuits behave unpredictably.
- Knowing which few numbers actually matter turns a scary document into a **two-minute lookup**.

### Intuitive Analogy
A datasheet is like the nutrition label and care instructions printed on
packaged food, all in one document. Almost nobody reads every line on a
cereal box, most people just check a couple of numbers that matter to
them (calories, sugar) and skip the rest. A datasheet works the same way,
it has far more information than any one project needs, and knowing which
handful of numbers to check is the actual skill.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A datasheet is the manufacturer's official document describing exactly what a component is, how it behaves, and its limits.
- The **pinout diagram** shows which physical pin or lead does what, essential for anything with more than two legs, like a chip or transistor.
- **Absolute maximum ratings** list the values that must never be exceeded (max voltage, max current, max temperature), going past these risks permanently damaging the part.
- **Typical or recommended operating values** are usually lower and safer than the absolute maximums, this is the range you actually want to design around.
- For an LED specifically, that means forward voltage and max forward current. For a capacitor, that means voltage rating and capacitance. For a resistor, that means resistance and power rating.
- Graphs showing behavior across temperature or frequency exist for advanced use cases, as a beginner it's fine to skip these entirely at first.
- When in doubt, search the datasheet for the word 'maximum' and the pinout diagram first, those two things answer most beginner questions.
- Datasheets for chips, not just simple parts, include a **pin function table**, describing what each pin does in plain language, separate from just the pinout diagram showing physical positions.
- Package information, like '5mm THT' or 'SOT-23', tells you the **physical size and mounting style**, which matters when planning a physical layout or checking whether a part will even fit where you intend to put it.
- Many datasheets include a **typical application circuit** diagram near the front or back, a ready-made example wiring for the most common use case, often the fastest way to get a new part working correctly the first time.

topics.title: Reading a Sensor: The General Pattern
topics.description: Almost every sensor follows the same three steps, **power it, read a pin, and convert that raw number** into something meaningful, no matter what it's actually measuring.

lesson.summary: Almost every sensor follows the same three steps, **power it, read a pin, and convert that raw number** into something meaningful, no matter what it's actually measuring.
lesson.content:
## Reading a Sensor: The General Pattern

> **Core Concept:** Almost every sensor follows the same three steps, **power it, read a pin, and convert that raw number** into something meaningful, no matter what it's actually measuring.

### Why It Matters
- There are thousands of different sensors (light, temperature, distance, sound), and it feels like you'd need to learn each one from scratch.
- A raw analogRead number like 612 means ==nothing on its own==, you need to know how to turn it into a real-world unit like degrees or lux.
- Without a general pattern, every new sensor datasheet feels intimidating instead of just a variation on something you already know.

### Intuitive Analogy
Reading almost any sensor is like using a kitchen scale that only shows a
number, not a unit. You still have to plug it in (power it), put something
on it (read it), and then translate that raw number using a conversion you
looked up (this reading means 250 grams, not just "612"). Every sensor,
fancy or simple, is doing that same three-step dance underneath, just with
a different conversion formula.


### Key Engineering Principles
- Step one is powering the sensor, most simple sensors just need a wire to 5V (or 3.3V) and a wire to ground, plus a signal wire to a pin, though some also need a pull-up or pull-down resistor on that signal wire, just like a button does.
- Step two is reading that signal pin, usually with analogRead for a sensor whose output varies continuously (like a light or temperature sensor), or digitalRead for a simple on/off sensor (like a magnetic door switch).
- Step three is converting the raw number into something meaningful, using a formula, a lookup table, or a library the sensor's manufacturer provides, this step is where a raw voltage reading becomes an actual real-world unit.
- A simple light sensor (photoresistor, also called an **LDR**) is a great example of a **voltage-divider** sensor, more light lowers its resistance, which changes the voltage at the midpoint of a divider formed with a fixed resistor, and analogRead sees that shifting voltage as a bigger or smaller raw number.
- The datasheet for any sensor is where the conversion formula, supply voltage range, and expected wiring live, it's worth checking even if the sensor 'looks' like one you've used before, since pinouts and formulas vary between otherwise similar-looking parts.
- Some sensors do the conversion for you over a digital protocol (like **I2C** or SPI), handing you an already-converted, calibrated number (like exact degrees or exact lux) instead of a raw voltage you'd have to interpret yourself, usually through a library the manufacturer provides.
- I2C sensors share just two wires (SDA for data, SCL for clock) across many devices at once, each identified by a unique address, which is why complex sensor boards (temperature, pressure, accelerometers) often use it instead of a dedicated analog pin per sensor.
- **Calibration** matters for real accuracy, many sensors ship with some manufacturing variation, and comparing a sensor's raw reading against a known reference value (like a real thermometer) lets you correct for that sensor's specific offset.
- Noisy raw readings are normal, not a sign something is broken, averaging several readings together (**oversampling**) or applying a simple moving average smooths out small fluctuations without needing new hardware.
- Response time varies by sensor type, a temperature sensor might take seconds to fully react to a change, while a light sensor reacts almost instantly, and code that reads too fast for the sensor's real response time can capture a misleadingly stale or transitional value.

topics.title: Resistors: the Traffic Control of a Circuit
topics.description: A **resistor**'s whole job is to limit **current** on purpose, so the rest of the circuit doesn't get more electricity than it can handle.

lesson.summary: A **resistor**'s whole job is to limit **current** on purpose, so the rest of the circuit doesn't get more electricity than it can handle.
lesson.content:
## Resistors: the Traffic Control of a Circuit

> **Core Concept:** A **resistor**'s whole job is to limit **current** on purpose, so the rest of the circuit doesn't get more electricity than it can handle.

### Why It Matters
- Most components (like LEDs) ==burn out almost instantly== if you hand them the full current a battery could push through them.
- You need a cheap, simple, predictable way to hold current down to a safe number without building anything complicated.
- Reading a resistor's value off its **color bands** looks like a secret code until you know the pattern.

### Intuitive Analogy
Think of a resistor like a deliberately narrow doorway at a concert exit. The
crowd (current) wants to rush out, but the narrow doorway forces only so many
people through per second, no matter how badly they want to leave. Make the
doorway narrower (higher resistance) and fewer people get through per second.
Widen it (lower resistance) and more do.


### Key Engineering Principles
- A resistor's value is measured in **ohms (Ω)**, and it directly limits current through **Ohm's law**: more resistance at the same voltage means less current. A 220Ω resistor on a 9V supply limits current very differently than a 10kΩ resistor on that same 9V.
- The most common reason to add a resistor is protecting an LED. Without one, an LED pulls way more current than it can survive and ==burns out in seconds==, since an LED's own resistance is very low and drops sharply the instant it turns on.
- Resistors have colored bands printed on them that encode their exact value, so you can read it without a multimeter once you know the code. Four-band resistors are the most common on hobbyist kits.
- The first two (or three, on five-band resistors) bands give the significant digits, the next band is a **multiplier** (how many zeros to add), and the last band is the **tolerance** (how far the real value might differ from the printed one, commonly gold for 5% or silver for 10%).
- Resistors don't care which direction current flows through them, unlike an LED or diode. You can install one either way around, there is **no wrong orientation**.
- **Power rating** matters too: a resistor also has a maximum wattage it can dissipate as heat before it's damaged, separate from its ohm value. Most hobbyist resistors are rated for 1/4 watt, which is plenty for small LED circuits but not for everything.
- Choosing a resistor value for an LED is a real calculation, not a guess: (Supply voltage minus the LED's forward voltage) divided by the LED's desired current gives the resistor value in ohms. A 9V supply, a 2V red LED, and a target of 20mA works out to about **350Ω**, so a standard 330Ω or 390Ω resistor would both be reasonable choices.
- Resistors can be combined: two in **series** add their resistance directly, two in **parallel** result in a combined resistance lower than either one alone. This matters when you need a value that isn't a standard off-the-shelf size.
- Surface-mount resistors (the tiny rectangular ones on modern circuit boards) use printed numbers instead of color bands, but encode the exact same digit-multiplier-tolerance idea.

topics.title: Serial Communication: UART
topics.description: **UART** sends data one bit at a time, one wire in each direction, with both sides simply agreeing in advance on how fast to talk.

lesson.summary: **UART** sends data one bit at a time, one wire in each direction, with both sides simply agreeing in advance on how fast to talk.
lesson.content:
## Serial Communication: UART

> **Core Concept:** **UART** sends data one bit at a time, one wire in each direction, with both sides simply agreeing in advance on how fast to talk.

### Why It Matters
- Two chips (or a chip and a computer) often need to exchange data, like text or sensor readings, but running a separate wire for every single bit at once would be expensive and impractical.
- You need a dead-simple way to move data between two devices using the fewest possible wires.
- Every microcontroller board's USB connection to your computer relies on this exact idea underneath, so understanding it demystifies the humble Serial Monitor.

### Intuitive Analogy
Imagine two people communicating with a single string of flags they raise
one at a time, instead of shouting a whole sentence at once. Both people
agreed beforehand exactly how long to hold up each flag before checking the
next one. As long as both sides keep that same timing, one flag at a time
still spells out a full message, it's just slower than saying it all in one
breath. That shared timing agreement is the whole trick.


### Key Engineering Principles
- UART stands for universal asynchronous receiver/transmitter, a piece of hardware built into most microcontrollers that handles sending and receiving data one bit at a time.
- It's **asynchronous**, meaning there's no separate clock wire shared between the two devices, both sides just agree in advance on a **baud rate** (how many bits per second) and time their bits based on that.
- A UART connection typically uses just two data wires: **TX** (transmit, this device's outgoing data) and **RX** (receive, this device's incoming data). TX on one device connects to RX on the other.
- Data is sent as a small packet per byte: a start bit signals the beginning, then the actual data bits, then usually a stop bit signals the end.
- ==If both sides don't agree on the exact same baud rate==, the receiving side reads the bits at the wrong moments and the data comes out as garbage.
- 9600 and 115200 baud are common speeds, but the exact number matters less than both sides matching it exactly.
- This is the same mechanism behind your microcontroller's USB Serial Monitor, USB just wraps a UART-like connection so it can talk to your computer.
- A byte's start bit is always a LOW pulse for one bit period, which is what lets the idle line (held HIGH between bytes) and the beginning of new data be told apart, the receiver watches for that falling edge to know when to start counting bits.
- Beyond start and stop bits, UART framing can include an optional parity bit, a simple error check that sets one extra bit so the total number of 1-bits in the byte is even or odd, letting the receiver catch some single-bit transmission errors.
- Framing is configurable and usually written as a shorthand like 8N1, meaning 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit, both devices must agree on this framing just as strictly as they must agree on baud rate.
- Because there's no shared clock, both devices' internal clocks drift slightly on their own, UART tolerates a small amount of that drift (roughly a few percent) since each bit's timing is only measured relative to the start bit, not accumulated across the whole byte.
- UART has no built-in error correction and no acknowledgment mechanism, if a byte arrives corrupted or is missed entirely, the receiver has no automatic way to know or ask for it again, any reliability has to be built on top in software.
